summaries.example: Imagine a basket with three apples. The sentence “every apple is red” is true only if all three apples are red. “Some apple is red” is true if at least one is red. The words “every” and “some” tell us how many things we are talking about.
summaries.summary: Quantification is the study of words and symbols that speak about whole groups or about whether at least one thing has a certain feature. In everyday language, words such as “all,” “each,” “some,” “many,” “most,” and “few” do this work. Logic turns some of these ideas into a careful formal language. The symbols ∀ and ∃ are commonly used for “everything” and “something.” A sentence such as “some apples are delicious” can be represented by saying that there is an object that is both an apple and delicious. A sentence such as “every material object is extended” can be represented by saying that everything that is a material object is extended. However, “most” and “few” do not fit this simple pattern. They compare parts of a group, so they are studied as generalized quantifiers. A formal logic also needs rules for forming sentences, rules for making proofs, and models that explain truth. Classical quantificational logic has important results called soundness and completeness: its proofs do not lead beyond what is true in all models, and every formula true in all models can be proved. Philosophers also study alternatives and extensions, including empty domains, intuitionistic logic, many-sorted logic, second-order quantification, and quantification used in questions about existence.
key_ideas: Words such as “all,” “each,” “some,” “most,” and “few” express generality about groups.
Modern logic often uses ∀ for “everything” or “every” and ∃ for “something” or “some.”
A logical system has a language, rules for proving statements, and interpretations that explain when statements are true.
A model gives a domain of things and explains which things fit each predicate.
Some systems use different rules for empty groups, possible proofs, or words that do not name anything.
Quantifiers can also help philosophers ask what kinds of things exist.
summaries.why_it_matters: Quantifiers help us make clear claims about groups instead of relying on vague wording. They are important in mathematics, computer science, language study, and philosophy. Formal logic can show whether a conclusion really follows from some starting statements. It also helps us notice hidden choices: for example, whether a group may be empty, what a word must name, and what things a theory says exist.

important_terms.definition: A word or symbol that tells us about a group, such as all, some, most, or few.
The things being talked about in a statement. It might be apples, animals, numbers, or something else.
A statement about a thing or group, such as “is red” or “is larger than.”
A symbol or rule used in logic to show that a statement is true for every thing in the domain.
A symbol or rule used in logic to show that a statement is true for at least one thing in the domain.

questions_to_think_about: Does “all” always mean all things, or can it mean all things in a particular group?
Can “every apple is red” be true when there are no apples?
What is the difference between “some,” “most,” and “all”?
Why might a logician want symbols instead of ordinary words?
When we say that something exists, what are we claiming?

summaries.example: Consider the statements “Some planets are visible to the naked eye” and “Most planets are visible to the naked eye.” The first can be formalized using an existential quantifier: there is an object that is both a planet and visible. The second cannot be captured simply by saying that most things are planets and visible, or that most things are visible if they are planets. It compares the visible planets with the planets that are not visible. This is why “most” is treated as a genuinely binary generalized quantifier.
summaries.summary:
Quantification studies the logical structure of generality. Natural-language determiners such as “all,” “each,” “some,” “many,” “most,” and “few” combine with noun phrases and predicates to make claims about restricted groups. Classical quantificational logic concentrates on the unary quantifiers ∀ and ∃. In its familiar treatment, “some A is B” becomes ∃x(Ax ∧ Bx), while “every A is B” becomes ∀x(Ax → Bx). The variable x ranges over a domain, and the predicates A and B determine subsets or relations within that domain. This treatment is powerful enough to represent a large amount of mathematical reasoning, but it does not reduce “most,” “many,” and “few” to the same simple pattern. Generalized quantifier theory instead analyzes such expressions by conditions on, or relations between, predicate extensions.

The entry also explains the formal machinery behind quantificational logic. A language is built from variables, predicate letters, connectives, and quantifiers. Axioms and inference rules define a proof system. A model supplies a nonempty domain and an interpretation for predicates; assignments give values to variables. Truth is then defined recursively. Soundness says that derivable formulas are valid, and completeness says that valid formulas are derivable. Compactness says that if every finite part of a set of formulas can be satisfied, the whole set can be satisfied. The entry surveys alternatives such as inclusive or free logic, intuitionistic quantification, and substitutional quantification, as well as extensions including many-sorted, second-order, plural, propositional, and generalized quantification. It finally connects quantification with debates about existence, ontology, modality, and time.
key_ideas: Frege and Russell helped establish a modern treatment in which binary expressions such as “some A are B” are represented using unary quantifiers plus predicates: ∃x(Ax ∧ Bx) and ∀x(Ax → Bx).
This reduction does not adequately represent “most,” “many,” or “few,” which motivates generalized quantifier theory.
A formal language contains variables, predicates, connectives, and quantifiers; rules determine which strings count as formulas and which inferences are permitted.
Tarskian model theory explains truth by specifying a domain, predicate extensions, and assignments of objects to variables.
Classical quantificational logic is sound and complete, and it also has compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem results.
Alternative systems alter the axioms or model theory, while extensions add new kinds of quantification, such as over predicates or different sorts of objects.
summaries.why_it_matters: Quantificational logic is a bridge between ordinary language, mathematics, and metaphysics. It lets us distinguish the structure of an argument from the particular topic being discussed. Its model theory gives precise ways to test truth and consequence, while its metatheorems explain the limits and strengths of formal proof. Philosophically, the choice between objectual, substitutional, plural, or higher-order quantification can affect what a theory appears to say exists. The study of quantifiers therefore concerns both how language works and how formal theories represent reality.

important_terms.definition: An expression of generality, such as “all,” “some,” “most,” or “few,” whose logical behavior can be studied formally.
A formal system in which variables range over objects and predicates express properties or relations of those objects; it is also called first-order or predicate logic.
The quantifier ∀, read as “for every” or “everything,” which requires a formula to hold throughout the domain.
The quantifier ∃, read as “there exists” or “something,” which requires a formula to hold for at least one member of the domain.
A specified collection over which variables range in an interpretation of a formal language.
A pair consisting of a nonempty domain and an interpretation that assigns extensions to predicates and meanings to other symbols.
The property that every theorem proved by a system is true in every model of the system.
The property that every formula true in every model is derivable in the formal system.

questions_to_think_about: Why does “some A is B” translate naturally as ∃x(Ax ∧ Bx), while “most A are B” require a comparison between sets?
What philosophical consequences follow from requiring classical models to have nonempty domains?
How do soundness and completeness connect formal proof with semantic truth?
Does quantifying over predicates in second-order logic add genuine expressive power, or can it be understood as quantification over sets?
When a theory entails ∃xFx, what does that suggest about its ontological commitments?

summaries.example: A class has 20 students. If 12 students bring a notebook, then “some students brought notebooks” is true, and “most students brought notebooks” may also be true. But “every student brought a notebook” is false. Notice that “most” is not just “most things are students and brought notebooks.” It compares notebook-bringing students with students who did not bring notebooks. This helps explain why logic treats “most” differently from the simpler quantifiers “some” and “every.”
summaries.summary:
Quantification is the study of expressions that tell us how broadly a statement applies. In English, “all,” “each,” “some,” “many,” “most,” and “few” are common examples. They usually work with a restricted noun phrase: “some apples,” “every material object,” or “most planets.” A useful formal idea is that “every” and “some” relate two predicates. “Some A is B” says that at least one thing is both A and B. “Every A is B” says that anything that is A is also B. Modern logic writes the relevant ideas with ∃ and ∀, rather than treating “every” and “some” as completely separate special forms.

Classical quantificational logic, also called first-order or predicate logic, supplies a formal language, axioms, and inference rules. Its variables range over a domain, and its predicates are interpreted as properties or relations in that domain. A model is used to define truth. An assignment gives objects to variables, and the clauses for connectives and quantifiers explain when a formula is satisfied. The system is sound and complete: proof and truth in all models match in the relevant ways. It also has compactness, meaning that satisfiability of every finite part is enough for satisfiability of the whole set, and a Löwenheim–Skolem result concerning countable models.

The entry also presents alternatives. Inclusive logic allows an empty domain, while free logic can allow singular terms that fail to denote. Intuitionistic logic connects truth with what can be constructed or proved, so its treatment of ∃ and ∀ differs from the classical treatment. Substitutional quantification tests formulas by replacing a variable with suitable expressions rather than assigning objects directly. key_ideas: Quantifier expressions make general statements and usually work with a restricted group, such as “some apples” or “every material object.”
Aristotle studied patterns involving statements such as all, some, no, and not all; modern quantificational logic later became better suited to mathematical reasoning.
Modern logic uses unary quantifiers ∀ and ∃, and can represent “some A is B” and “every A is B” with predicates and connectives.
A model includes a domain and an interpretation of predicates. A formula is valid when it is true in every model.
Classical quantificational logic has soundness, completeness, compactness, and Löwenheim–Skolem results.
Philosophers disagree about how to handle empty domains, non-denoting terms, constructive proof, and quantification over predicates or propositions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Quantifiers affect both everyday reasoning and advanced theories. They help us see whether an argument depends on “all,” “some,” or a comparison such as “most.” Formal logic makes those differences exact and provides methods for checking consequences. Its variations also reveal that choices about domains, names, proof, and interpretation are not merely technical: they can change what a logical theory can express and what it appears to claim about existence.

important_terms.definition: A word or symbol that describes how many members of a group a statement concerns, such as all, some, most, or few.
The collection of objects that variables are allowed to range over in a logical interpretation.
A property or relation represented by a predicate, such as “is a student” or “likes.”
A formal rule or system used to determine which conclusions follow from given statements.
A model’s assignment of a meaning or extension to each nonlogical symbol, such as a predicate.
A result saying that everything provable in a logical system is true in all of its models.
A result saying that every formula true in all models can be proved using the system’s rules.
A study of quantifiers whose meanings cannot all be handled by only the ordinary “every” and “some” patterns.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a statement about “every member of a group” be true when the group has no members?
What is gained by replacing ordinary phrases with symbols such as ∀ and ∃?
Can a formal system be complete without being able to express every useful kind of quantifier?
Is quantifying over words or sentences the same as quantifying over the objects those words describe?
How might a theory’s choice of domain affect what it says exists?
